text: Raw billing and usage data is now landing in Snowflake, but it's exactly as messy as any raw source -- different id names for the same person, amounts stored as strings, nothing deduplicated. This lesson builds the dbt project that turns it into Driftwood's trusted marts.

Driftwood's dbt project, driftwood_analytics, is organized the way the dbt course taught: staging cleans and renames with no business logic yet, intermediate joins and applies rules, marts are the final consumable tables -- browsable here in the real dbt IDE.
Running dbt build picks up every model in dependency order -- the same real dbt run output you'd see building Driftwood's own staging, intermediate, and marts models in sequence.

Staging just cleans and renames. stg_billing_events converts amount and timestamp safely so a bad row becomes a visible NULL a test can catch, not a failed run. stg_usage_events renames user_id to subscriber_id right here, once, reconciling the two source systems' different names for the same person instead of re-deriving that fix in every downstream query.

Intermediate is where billing and usage data actually meet for the first time. int_subscriber_activity joins the two staging models on subscriber and day, using ref() instead of a hardcoded table name -- that's what lets dbt build this dependency graph automatically.
dbt turns every one of those ref() calls into a real, browsable lineage graph -- exactly the dependency chain Driftwood's own staging-to-marts layering produces.

Marts are what Power BI and analysts actually query. fct_subscriptions is a fact table, one row per subscription event; dim_subscribers is a dimension table, one row per subscriber, with the first-seen and cancellation timestamps Lesson 8's churn measure depends on.
Next lesson: testing and documenting this project, so a mistake here gets caught before it ever reaches the dashboard.
